paragraphs: (The sons of Zakkai, Ezra 2:9.) (A Tanna of a baraita.) He was a student of Rabbi Shimon, as in Shabbat 79b, where he spoke in his name. Seder HaDorot cites the wording of Yuchasin: “Rabbi Zakkai, chapter HaMotzi Yayin, a Tanna of a baraita, a student of Rabbi Shimon Berabbi”; Hyman considers this a scribal error. Yuchasin HaShalem has “a student of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehudah”; Hyman likewise calls that an error and proposes that “a student of Rabbi Shimon ברב״י” lost its abbreviation marks; Hyman identifies him as Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai. In Berakhot 25a he disagrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and in Niddah 23b he disagrees with Rabbi; this is why Yuchasin HaShalem wrote that he was a colleague of our holy Rabbi. In Jerusalem Talmud Niddah, chapter 3, end of halakhah 2, Rabbi Yochanan spoke in his name (the Niddah statement). In Megillah 27b his students asked him: “By what merit did you live long?” He said to them: “In my days … I never neglected the sanctification of the day. I had an old mother; once she sold the kerchief on her head and brought me [wine for] the sanctification of the day.” It was taught: when she died she left him three hundred jugs of wine; when he died he left his sons three thousand jugs of wine.

notes.text: The supplied ברב״י abbreviation is retained before Hyman’s proposed ben Yochai interpretation; Berabbi and ben Yehudah are competing reported readings. His lost-marks explanation and identity conclusion remain attributed, not newly pixel-proved.

Megillah 27b directly names Zakkai and gives the mother’s head-covering and the 300/3000 wine-jug sequence. It does not verify the precise Yuchasin editions, Hyman’s lost-abbreviation-marks explanation or his identification with Shimon ben Yochai; those remain his arguments. Ezra’s sons of Zakkai are a cited namesake notice, not an identity admission.
